questions.stem: An 84-year-old client with dementia-related psychosis has a new order for quetiapine. The potassium is 3.0 mEq/L, and the client also takes sotalol. Which action should the nurse take before the first dose?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Administer the first dose because quetiapine is approved for agitation associated with dementia when nonpharmacologic measures have not controlled the behavior.","B":"Clarify the order before the first dose because quetiapine is not approved for dementia-related psychosis, and hypokalemia plus sotalol increase torsades risk.","C":"Give the first dose and replace potassium afterward because correction of an electrolyte abnormality is not relevant to quetiapine-associated QT risk.","D":"Use the medication after documenting the QTc because the dementia mortality warning and electrolyte abnormalities do not require prescriber review before the first dose."}}
questions.rationale: Current quetiapine labeling carries a boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis and states that quetiapine is not approved for that indication. The label also advises avoiding quetiapine in circumstances that increase torsades or sudden-death risk, including hypokalemia and concomitant QT-prolonging drugs. This client has both risk factors, so the nurse should clarify the order and risk-management plan before administration rather than treating the QTc value in isolation.
questions.source_detail: Revised May 2026: boxed warning for dementia-related psychosis; QT section advises avoiding hypokalemia and concomitant QT-prolonging drugs.

questions.stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick from a used hollow-bore needle. The source patient’s bloodborne-infection status is not yet known. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Squeeze the puncture until it bleeds freely, apply a concentrated antiseptic, and wait for the source patient’s laboratory results before reporting the exposure.","B":"Cover the puncture with an occlusive dressing and finish the current medication round, then report the exposure at the end of the shift if symptoms develop.","C":"Request testing of the source patient first and delay personal evaluation until infection status is confirmed, because prophylaxis is unnecessary after an unknown exposure.","D":"Wash the puncture site promptly with soap and water, report the exposure immediately, and obtain urgent occupational-exposure evaluation for indicated prophylaxis."}}
questions.rationale: OSHA directs workers with needlestick or blood exposure to immediately clean the wound with soap and water, report the incident immediately, and seek immediate medical attention. Post-exposure evaluation should not be delayed while waiting for the source patient’s test results because time-sensitive prophylaxis may be indicated. Squeezing the wound or delaying reporting does not replace prompt first aid and exposure evaluation.
questions.source_name: OSHA — Bloodborne Pathogens / Needlestick Exposure Guidance
questions.source_detail: Immediate wound cleaning with soap and water, immediate reporting, and immediate medical evaluation after occupational blood exposure.

questions.stem: A client will receive a newly inserted central venous catheter for prolonged IV therapy. Which insertion-and-maintenance plan best reflects current bloodstream-infection prevention guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Perform hand hygiene, use cap, mask, sterile gown, sterile gloves and a full-body drape, prepare the skin with chlorhexidine-alcohol, and reassess line need daily.","B":"Use chlorhexidine-alcohol and sterile gloves but omit the full-body sterile drape, because daily site care after insertion compensates for reduced insertion barriers.","C":"Use maximal sterile barriers but prepare the insertion site with alcohol alone, then replace the catheter on a fixed schedule to prevent colonization during therapy.","D":"Perform hand hygiene, use sterile gloves and a small fenestrated drape, cleanse with povidone-iodine, and plan to keep the line for the full antibiotic course."}}
questions.rationale: CDC central-line prevention guidance emphasizes hand hygiene, maximal sterile barrier precautions during insertion, chlorhexidine-based skin antisepsis, and prompt removal when a catheter is no longer essential. Maximal barrier precautions include cap, mask, sterile gown, sterile gloves, and a full-body sterile drape. Catheters should not be kept or routinely replaced solely according to a preset treatment duration when clinical necessity has changed.
questions.source_name: CDC — Intravascular Catheter-Related Infection Prevention Recommendations
questions.source_detail: Hand hygiene; maximal sterile barrier precautions; chlorhexidine skin antisepsis; prompt removal of unnecessary central catheters.

questions.stem: A nurse is leaving the room of a client on Airborne Precautions while wearing gloves, gown, eye protection, and a fit-tested N95 respirator. Which removal plan is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Remove the N95 respirator inside the room before touching the gown or gloves, then leave the room and complete the remaining PPE removal in the hallway.","B":"Keep the N95 on until the end of the shift and remove the gown and gloves after entering another patient-care area, reducing repeated donning and doffing.","C":"Remove contaminated PPE other than the respirator without self-contamination, clean the hands, exit and close the door, then remove the respirator and perform hand hygiene.","D":"Leave the room wearing all PPE, remove the respirator first in the hallway, and then return to the isolation area to discard the gown, gloves, and eye protection in the room."}}
questions.rationale: CDC core infection-control guidance directs healthcare personnel to remove and discard PPE other than respirators before leaving the patient room or care area. When a respirator is required, it is removed after leaving the room and closing the door, with hand hygiene performed during and after safe doffing according to the facility’s sequence. This avoids the brittle teaching that one universal item must always be removed first while preserving the critical airborne-precaution rule for respirators.
questions.source_name: CDC — Core Infection Prevention Practices and Airborne Precautions
questions.source_detail: Remove PPE other than respirators before leaving the room; remove the respirator after exiting and closing the door; perform hand hygiene and avoid self-contamination during doffing.

questions.stem: A fire alarm activates on an inpatient unit after smoke is reported in one patient room. Fire doors and suppression systems are functioning. Which response best reflects healthcare fire-safety principles?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Begin immediate building-wide evacuation of all patients regardless of location, because healthcare fire response requires complete evacuation as the first protective action.","B":"Follow the facility fire-response plan, use compartmentation to defend patients in place when safe, and relocate those in threatened areas as conditions require.","C":"Keep all patients in their current rooms until the fire department arrives, because compartmentation eliminates the need for relocation during a hospital fire.","D":"Open corridor doors throughout the unit to improve visibility and movement, then relocate patients before activating the hospital fire-response process."}}
questions.rationale: Healthcare occupancies are designed around compartmentation and a defend-in-place strategy rather than automatic whole-building evacuation. Joint Commission fire-safety guidance explains that protected compartments permit patients to remain in safe care areas while threatened patients can be relocated as the fire-response plan requires; full evacuation is a last resort when protection or conditions require it. Staff should follow the organization’s fire-response plan rather than apply a memorized acronym as a universal substitute for the actual emergency plan.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — Fire Protection and General Life-Safety Requirements
questions.source_detail: Healthcare occupancies use compartmentation and defend-in-place strategies; relocation may occur to safe areas and evacuation is a last resort depending on conditions.

questions.stem: A nurse gives a scheduled medication to the wrong client. The client is assessed promptly, the provider is notified, and no immediate harm is found. Which additional action best supports the organization’s patient-safety system?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Document only the clinical assessment and provider notification because a formal safety-event report is unnecessary when the client has no immediate adverse effect.","B":"Wait until the next shift to determine whether symptoms occur before reporting the error, because event systems are intended primarily for errors that cause harm.","C":"Discuss the error informally with the charge nurse but avoid entering it into the reporting system unless the provider specifically requests a formal report.","D":"Submit a patient-safety event report through the facility’s reporting process after the client has been assessed and immediate clinical needs have been addressed."}}
questions.rationale: Patient-safety event reporting systems are designed to capture errors, adverse events, near misses, and unsafe conditions so organizations can identify hazards and improve systems. AHRQ notes that frontline clinicians involved in medication errors commonly initiate these reports. Clinical assessment and communication about the patient’s immediate care come first; after those needs are addressed, the medication error should be submitted through the organization’s established safety-event reporting process rather than being handled only informally or reported only if harm appears.
questions.source_name: AHRQ PSNet — Reporting Patient Safety Events
questions.source_detail: Frontline personnel commonly submit event reports; medication errors are among the events frequently captured by hospital reporting systems for safety learning.

questions.stem: A tenfold medication overdose caused by a transcription error reaches a client and results in permanent neurologic impairment that is not related to the natural course of the illness. How should this event be classified under the current Joint Commission sentinel-event definition?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A near miss, because the transcription mistake occurred before the medication reached the client even though the overdose was subsequently administered.","B":"A routine medication variance, because medication errors are excluded from sentinel-event classification when a transcription step contributed to the error.","C":"A sentinel event, because the safety event reached the client and caused permanent harm that was not primarily related to the natural course of the illness.","D":"A no-harm event, because permanent neurologic injury is classified according to the underlying condition rather than the medication error that caused it."}}
questions.rationale: Under the current 2026 Joint Commission definition, a sentinel event is a patient safety event not primarily related to the natural course of the patient’s illness or underlying condition that reaches the patient and results in death, severe harm, or permanent harm. This medication overdose reached the client and caused permanent neurologic impairment, so it meets that definition. Joint Commission has announced changes to the sentinel-event framework for 2027, but those future changes are not the current standard in August 2026.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — Sentinel Event Policy and Procedures
questions.source_detail: Current 2026 definition: patient safety event that reaches the patient and results in death, severe harm, or permanent harm, not primarily due to the natural course of illness.

questions.stem: A postoperative client has had an indwelling urinary catheter for 5 days for strict intake-and-output monitoring. The client is now hemodynamically stable and no longer needs hourly urine measurements. Which action best supports CAUTI prevention?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Reassess the indication and advocate for prompt removal because strict postoperative output monitoring is no longer needed and duration increases CAUTI risk.","B":"Replace the catheter and drainage bag on a scheduled basis, then continue catheterization because routine replacement lowers CAUTI risk during extended postoperative use.","C":"Disconnect the drainage tubing for each output measurement so the catheter can remain in place while reducing urine stagnation in the collection system.","D":"Keep the catheter in place until discharge because five days of use has already established a closed system and removal could increase infection risk."}}
questions.rationale: CDC recommends leaving indwelling urinary catheters in place only as long as needed and removing postoperative catheters as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours when there is no continuing indication. Prolonged catheter duration is the most important CAUTI risk factor. The closed drainage system should be maintained, and routine fixed-interval catheter or bag replacement is not recommended. Once strict urine-output monitoring is no longer necessary, prompt removal is the priority.
questions.source_detail: Remove indwelling catheters as soon as they are no longer needed; maintain a closed drainage system; do not change catheters or bags at routine fixed intervals.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to scrub for a sterile surgical procedure. Jewelry has been removed and the hands and forearms are not visibly soiled. Which preparation is appropriate before donning sterile gloves?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Wash hands and forearms briefly with plain soap, dry them, and immediately don sterile gloves because routine handwashing is sufficient before surgical procedures.","B":"Use the routine alcohol hand sanitizer used between patient contacts and don sterile gloves while the hands remain moist, allowing the product to continue acting during surgery.","C":"Skip additional hand antisepsis because the sterile gown and gloves provide the required barrier, provided standard hand hygiene was performed earlier in the shift.","D":"Perform surgical hand antisepsis with antimicrobial soap for the labeled scrub time or an alcohol-based surgical hand rub with persistent activity, then dry before gloving."}}
questions.rationale: CDC recommends surgical hand antisepsis before donning sterile gloves for surgery. Acceptable methods include antimicrobial soap used for the manufacturer-recommended scrub time or an alcohol-based surgical hand-rub product with persistent activity used according to its instructions. When an alcohol-based surgical product is used, hands and forearms must be appropriately prepared and allowed to dry before sterile gloves are donned. Routine handwashing or ordinary patient-care sanitizer use is not a substitute for the surgical antisepsis protocol.
questions.source_name: CDC — Clinical Safety: Hand Hygiene for Healthcare Workers
questions.source_detail: Surgical hand antisepsis before sterile gloves; antimicrobial soap or alcohol-based surgical hand rub with persistent activity; allow hands/forearms to dry before gloving.
